title: Trier to Highgate: the Moor, the Spectre, and the Book
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Trier, the house in the Brückergasse
stops.campa: At two in the morning of the fifth of May, in the baroque house at Brückergasse 664, a son is born to the advocate Heinrich Marx and Henriette née Presburg. Trier is the oldest city of Germany, Roman before Rome fell, and on both sides the child descends from unbroken lines of rabbis: his grandfather Meier Halevi was rabbi of this very town, his uncle holds the office still. The father has lately crossed to the Prussian church so that he may keep his practice at the bar. They name the boy Karl. The Moselle runs past the walls, patient as history.
suggested_refs: The Karl-Marx-Haus at Brückenstraße 10, Trier, kept as a museum of his birth
sources: Heinz Monz, Karl Marx: Grundlagen der Entwicklung zu Leben und Werk

stops.name: Trier, the parlour baptism in the Simeonstraße
stops.campa: In the family's rooms near the Porta Nigra, no church, no crowd, the military chaplain Mühlenhoff pours the water of Prussian Christianity over Karl, six years old, and over his brothers and sisters with him. The father went first, years ago; the mother, whose parents still live in the old faith in Nijmegen, will wait until her own father dies. So the grandson of the rabbis of Trier becomes, on paper, an Evangelical Christian, and keeps for life the double sight of the man baptized at home: inside every congregation, belonging to none.
suggested_refs: The baptismal register of the Evangelical congregation of Trier, 26 August 1824
sources: jewinthepew.org, '26 August 1824: Baptism of Karl Marx'
Jonathan Sperber, Karl Marx: A Nineteenth-Century Life

stops.name: Trier, the walks with Baron von Westphalen
stops.campa: Ludwig von Westphalen, Prussian councillor, half a Scot by his mother's line of Argyll, takes the schoolboy walking through the vineyards and the Roman ruins above the Moselle. He recites Homer and whole scenes of Shakespeare from memory; he speaks of Saint-Simon and of the coming reign of association. Karl drinks it all. In the Baron's tall house he also finds the Baron's daughter Jenny, four years his elder, the most beautiful girl in Trier, the queen of its ballrooms. The old man is planting two loves at once: the Greeks, and her.
stops.quote: You, my fatherly friend, were always a living argumentum ad oculos to me, that idealism is no figment of the imagination, but a truth.
stops.quote_source: Dedication of his doctoral dissertation to Ludwig von Westphalen, 1841
suggested_refs: The dedication leaf of the doctoral dissertation, inscribed to Ludwig von Westphalen
sources: Franz Mehring, Karl Marx: Geschichte seines Lebens

stops.name: Trier, the Gymnasium and the examination essay
stops.campa: In the old Jesuit college that houses the Friedrich-Wilhelm-Gymnasium, the seventeen-year-old sits his leaving examinations under the liberal headmaster Wittenbach, whom the police already watch. For the German essay on the choice of a profession he writes a page that reads, afterwards, like a sealed prophecy: that a man cannot choose freely, that his relations in society have begun before he can determine them, and that the surest greatness belongs to the one who works for the whole. In October a boat carries him down the Moselle toward Bonn, and Trier keeps only his childhood.
stops.quote: The chief guide which must direct us in the choice of a profession is the welfare of mankind and our own perfection.
stops.quote_source: Abitur essay, 'Reflections of a Young Man on the Choice of a Profession', August 1835
suggested_refs: The manuscript of the Abitur essay of August 1835, preserved in the school records
sources: MECW vol. 1, 'Reflections of a Young Man on the Choice of a Profession'
Heinz Monz, Karl Marx und Trier

segments.name: Bonn and Berlin, the Student Years

stops.name: Bonn, matriculation at the university
stops.campa: Karl matriculates in the faculty of law in the yellow electoral palace on the Rhine, and immediately studies everything except law: nine courses, Greek mythology, Homer, art history, verse. He joins the Poets' Club, where the police keep a list of names, and the Trier Tavern Club, where they keep a tab; the Landsmannschaft of his home town soon makes him one of its presidents. His father writes anxious, loving letters about money and moderation. The boy answers with poems. The Rhine at Bonn is broad and bright and full of student songs, and he sings them.
suggested_refs: The 1836 lithograph of the Trier Tavern Club at Bonn, Marx among the students
sources: University of Bonn matriculation register, 17 October 1835
David McLellan, Karl Marx: His Life and Thought

stops.name: Bonn, the Karzer and the duel
stops.campa: The wild year ripens. In June the university locks him a night in the Karzer, the student prison, for drunkenness and nocturnal uproar: visitors climb in through the window with more wine, as the custom is. Then the aristocratic Corps Borussia, Prussians who make the plebeian Trier boys kiss the ground, provoke him once too often; Karl fights a sabre duel with one of them and carries away a cut above the left eye. His father, horrified, asks whether duelling is so interwoven with philosophy, and pulls him out of Bonn to sober Berlin.
suggested_refs: The university Karzer of old Bonn, its walls scrawled with the names of imprisoned students
sources: Heinrich Marx to Karl, letters of 1836 (MEGA III/1)

stops.name: Trier, the secret betrothal to Jenny von Westphalen
stops.campa: Home for the vacation between Bonn and Berlin, the eighteen-year-old wins what the ballrooms of the Rhineland could not: Jenny von Westphalen, the baron's daughter, breaks with a promising lieutenant and pledges herself in secret to the advocate's son, four years her junior, penniless, Jewish-born, incandescent. Her family must not know yet; only his father is told, and keeps the secret like contraband. The engagement will last seven clandestine years and cost her battles against her own blood. From Berlin he will send her three volumes of poems, oceans of them, all fire.
stops.quote: I can assure you, without the slightest romanticism, that I am head over heels in love, and indeed in the most serious way. I have been engaged for more than seven years, and my fiancée has fought the fiercest battles for me.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Arnold Ruge, 13 March 1843
suggested_refs: The portrait of the young Jenny von Westphalen, the most beautiful girl in Trier

stops.name: Berlin, the university on Unter den Linden
stops.campa: He matriculates in law at the university of Hegel, dead five years and reigning still. Savigny lectures him on jurisprudence, Eduard Gans on the rational march of history; the city itself, barracks and ministries and sand, is a workhouse compared with the Rhine. Karl reads until his health cracks: he attempts a philosophy of law in three hundred pages and burns it, writes poems to the absent Jenny, sleeps little. Berlin will hold him six years and turn the poet into a dialectician. He leaves love behind him in Trier and walks into the cold light of the concept.
stops.quote: There are moments in one's life which are like frontier posts marking the completion of a period but at the same time clearly indicating a new direction.
stops.quote_source: Letter to his father, 10 November 1837
suggested_refs: The main building of the Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität on Unter den Linden, Berlin
sources: University of Berlin matriculation register, 22 October 1836
Marx to his father, 10 November 1837 (MECW vol. 1)

stops.name: Stralau, the fishing village and the conversion to Hegel
stops.campa: Broken by overwork, the doctor orders him out of the city, and Karl lodges in the fishing village of Stralau on its green spit between the Spree and the Rummelsburg lake. Walking the shore to Berlin and back, lungs filling, he wrestles the philosophy he had meant to despise. He has read fragments of Hegel and disliked its grotesque craggy melody; now, in convalescence, he reads it end to end, and the enemy takes the fortress from within. He returns to town a Hegelian, chained, as he writes, to the ship like a lover to his mistress.
stops.quote: A curtain had fallen, my holy of holies was rent asunder, and new gods had to be installed... I arrived at the point of seeking the idea in the real itself.
stops.quote_source: Letter to his father, 10 November 1837
suggested_refs: The Stralau peninsula on the Spree, site of the fishermen's village of his convalescence
sources: Marx to his father, 10 November 1837 (MECW vol. 1)
David McLellan, Karl Marx: His Life and Thought

stops.name: Berlin, the Doctors' Club and the doctorate of Prometheus
stops.campa: In Hippel's wine-cellar on the Friedrichstraße the Young Hegelians hold their symposium: Bruno Bauer, Köppen, Rutenberg; and the youngest of the Doctors' Club out-argues the doctors. His father has died; Prussia's new king is hounding Hegel's left-hand children out of every chair. Karl writes his dissertation on Democritus and Epicurus, the physics of falling atoms and the swerve of freedom, and prefixes to it a hymn to the fire-thief. The University of Jena, sight unseen, sends him the doctor's diploma on the fifteenth of April. No German lectern will ever hold him.
stops.quote: Prometheus is the most eminent saint and martyr in the philosophical calendar.
stops.quote_source: Foreword to the doctoral dissertation, 1841
suggested_refs: The Jena doctoral diploma of 15 April 1841, awarded in absentia
sources: Difference Between the Democritean and Epicurean Philosophy of Nature (MECW vol. 1)

stops.name: Cologne, the Rheinische Zeitung and the freedom of the press
stops.campa: Rhenish merchants and bankers have founded a liberal paper in Cologne, and from Trier and Bonn the young doctor begins to feed it thunder. His first great series, running from his twenty-fourth birthday, defends the freedom of the press against the Rhine Province Assembly with a wit the censors cannot quite catch in their nets. Readers ask who the anonymous Rhinelander is. The paper's circulation climbs. Cologne, cathedral crane frozen over the roofs, steamers on the river, money and Catholicism, becomes the arena where German philosophy first walks out of the seminar and into the street.
stops.quote: The free press is the ubiquitous vigilant eye of a people's soul, the embodiment of a people's faith in itself.
stops.quote_source: Rheinische Zeitung, debates on freedom of the press, May 1842
suggested_refs: A surviving number of the Rheinische Zeitung für Politik, Handel und Gewerbe, Cologne 1842
sources: marxists.org, 'Proceedings of the Sixth Rhine Province Assembly'

stops.name: Cologne: editor-in-chief, and the theft of wood
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of October Marx takes the editor's chair, and the moderate sheet becomes the most dangerous paper in Prussia; within months its circulation triples. He writes on the law against the gathering of fallen wood, by which the poor of the Moselle are made criminals for the customary rights of centuries, and on the misery of the wine-growers of his home valley. Here, he will say ever after, the philosopher first stubbed his toe on economics. In November a cool young Englishman-from-Barmen named Engels calls at the office; the editor receives him with reserve.
stops.quote: In the year 1842-43, as editor of the Rheinische Zeitung, I first found myself in the embarrassing position of having to discuss what is known as material interests.
stops.quote_source: Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, 1859
suggested_refs: The articles on the law on thefts of wood, Rheinische Zeitung, October-November 1842

stops.name: Cologne, the censor wins; the editor resigns
stops.campa: The Tsar himself has complained of the Cologne paper; Berlin appoints censor upon censor, and a cabinet order kills the Rheinische Zeitung with effect from April. On the seventeenth of March Marx lays down the editorship in a printed declaration, hoping in vain that the sacrifice will save the paper. He is twenty-four and has learned the whole anatomy of the Prussian state from inside its muzzle. Shareholders mourn; the censor Saint-Paul reports with relief that the spiritus rector is gone. Marx packs for the Baths of Kreuznach, where Jenny is waiting, and for the world.
stops.quote: I have become tired of hypocrisy, stupidity, gross arbitrariness, and of our bowing and scraping, dodging, and hair-splitting over words. Consequently, the government has given me back my freedom.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Arnold Ruge, 25 January 1843
suggested_refs: Marx's printed declaration of resignation from the Rheinische Zeitung, 17 March 1843

stops.name: Bad Kreuznach, the wedding in the Pauluskirche
stops.campa: After seven years of secret constancy, Karl Marx and Jenny von Westphalen are married on the nineteenth of June in the Pauluskirche at Kreuznach on the Nahe, where the widowed baroness has taken her daughter. The bride is twenty-nine, the groom twenty-five and without position, prospects, or country worth keeping. They honeymoon along the Rhine; the money-box stands open on the coach seat and friends and beggars help themselves. All summer in Kreuznach he fills notebooks: Hegel's philosophy of the state turned on its head, history of France, history of revolution, the trousseau he brings to Paris.
stops.quote: ...the ruthless criticism of all that exists, ruthless both in the sense of not being afraid of the results it arrives at and in the sense of being just as little afraid of conflict with the powers that be.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Arnold Ruge, Kreuznach, September 1843
suggested_refs: The Pauluskirche at Bad Kreuznach and the marriage register of 19 June 1843
sources: Letters from the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher (MECW vol. 3)

stops.name: Paris, arrival in the capital of the new world
stops.campa: At the end of October the young couple reaches Paris, capital of every revolution since 1789, and lodges in the rue Vanneau in the Faubourg Saint-Germain: first in Ruge's short-lived commune of German families at number 23, soon in their own rooms at number 38. Marx has come to co-edit the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher, the arranged marriage of German philosophy and French politics. He plunges into the emigrant workers' societies and the socialist salons, meets Proudhon and argues Hegel at him through whole nights, and reads political economy with a new and terrible appetite.
stops.quote: We do not confront the world in a doctrinaire way with a new principle: Here is the truth, kneel down before it! We develop new principles for the world out of the world's own principles.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Arnold Ruge, September 1843, printed in the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher
suggested_refs: The rue Vaneau in the seventh arrondissement, the Marx household of 1843-1845

stops.name: Paris, the Jahrbücher and the opium of the people
stops.campa: The one and only double issue of the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher appears at the end of February: Heine's satires, Engels's outline of a critique of political economy, which the editor reads like a man struck, and Marx's own introduction on Hegel's philosophy of right, where religion is named the sigh of the oppressed creature and the proletariat steps onstage for the first time as the class whose chains are radical. Prussia bans the journal, seizes copies at the border, and issues warrants for the editors' arrest. Marx can no longer go home. The exile has begun.
stops.quote: Religion is the sigh of the oppressed creature, the heart of a heartless world, and the soul of soulless conditions. It is the opium of the people.
stops.quote_source: Introduction to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher, February 1844
suggested_refs: The single double issue of the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher, Paris 1844

stops.name: Paris, the Café de la Régence: ten days with Engels
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of August, at the Café de la Régence by the Palais-Royal, the chess café of Diderot and Bonaparte, Friedrich Engels, returning from Manchester with the condition of the English working class in his notebooks, sits down opposite the man who once received him coldly in Cologne. This time the pieces fit. Ten days of talk in the café and at the rue Vanneau, and they find themselves in agreement in all theoretical fields; the collaboration begun over these tables will end only at Highgate. All summer Marx has been filling the manuscripts on estranged labour.
suggested_refs: The Café de la Régence by the Palais-Royal, where the forty-year alliance began
sources: Engels, 'On the History of the Communist League' (1885)
Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 (MECW vol. 3)
Gareth Stedman Jones, Karl Marx: Greatness and Illusion

stops.name: Paris, the order of Guizot
stops.campa: Prussia leans on France over the émigré weekly Vorwärts!, in which Marx has hailed the revolt of the Silesian weavers, and on the twenty-fifth of January Guizot's ministry signs the expulsion of its German contributors. Marx has a week. Heine, whom he has come to love and cannot pack, stays behind with his mattress-grave still years away; Jenny, with the baby Jennychen, sells the furniture and follows in the snow. On the first of February the coach rolls north through frost toward Belgium. Paris has made him: he arrived a philosopher and leaves a communist.
stops.quote: Of all the people I am leaving behind here, those I leave with most regret are the Heines. I would gladly include you in my luggage!
stops.quote_source: Letter to Heinrich Heine, Paris, end of January 1845
suggested_refs: Vorwärts! Pariser Deutsche Zeitschrift, the banned weekly of 1844

stops.name: Brussels, the Bois Sauvage and the pledge
stops.campa: In early February the expelled editor reaches Brussels through the snow and takes rooms at the Hôtel du Bois Sauvage in the shadow of Sainte-Gudule. Little Belgium, constitutional and nervous, will tolerate the famous red doctor on one condition: in March he signs, on his word of honour, an undertaking to publish nothing on the politics of the day. He signs, and prepares, in perfect keeping of the letter, the most political book of the century. Jenny arrives exhausted with the baby; Engels soon takes the house next to theirs and hands over the royalties of his book.
stops.quote: I engage upon my word of honour not to publish in Belgium any work on current politics.
stops.quote_source: Written pledge to the Belgian authorities, Brussels, 22 March 1845
suggested_refs: The Hôtel du Bois Sauvage on the Place Sainte-Gudule, first and last of his Brussels addresses
sources: Belgian Sûreté publique file on Marx, 1845-1848
the-low-countries.com, 'Karl Marx Wrote Global History in Brussels'

stops.name: Saint-Josse-ten-Noode, rue de l'Alliance 5: the eleventh thesis
stops.campa: The family settles at number 5 in the rue de l'Alliance by the Leuven gate, Engels at number 7, wall to wall. In a pocket notebook this spring Marx jots eleven theses on Feuerbach, a page of lightning that ends with the sentence engraved later on his tomb. Through the winter that follows, he and Engels pile up the great unprintable manuscript of the German Ideology, in which history is stood at last on its feet: life determines consciousness. Laura is born here; in December Marx renounces his Prussian citizenship forever. The two households hold one long seminar.
stops.quote: The philosophers have only interpreted the world, in various ways; the point is to change it.
stops.quote_source: Theses on Feuerbach, XI, Brussels notebook of spring 1845
suggested_refs: The notebook page of the Theses on Feuerbach, in Marx's hand

stops.name: Manchester, the desk in the alcove at Chetham's
stops.campa: In July Engels leads him across the Channel to England: Marx's first sight of the country whose economy he will anatomize for forty years. Six weeks in London and Manchester: in the medieval library of Chetham's, oldest free library of the English-speaking world, the two sit at a small four-sided desk in a bay window, working through the economists, Petty, Cooper, Thompson, whose excerpts fill the Manchester notebooks. A quarter-century later Engels will sit at the same desk and write to Marx that the coloured glass still makes the same weather. The desk remains.
suggested_refs: The economists' alcove desk in Chetham's Library, Manchester, preserved as they used it
sources: Chetham's Library, Manchester, visitor records and tradition

stops.name: Ixelles, rue d'Orléans 42: the poverty of philosophy
stops.campa: In October 1846 the growing family moves to a small, poorly furnished house at 42 rue d'Orléans in Ixelles. From here Marx runs the Communist Correspondence Committee, threads letters to London, Paris and Cologne, and excommunicates the tailor-prophet Weitling across a green table, Weitling complaining afterward that he had never seen such fury over doctrine. When Proudhon publishes his Philosophy of Poverty, Marx answers in French, within months, with the Poverty of Philosophy, his first mature economics in print. Edgar is born in this house; the mill-wheel of the epigram turns in it.
stops.quote: The hand-mill gives you society with the feudal lord; the steam-mill, society with the industrial capitalist.
stops.quote_source: The Poverty of Philosophy, 1847
suggested_refs: The commemorative plaque at rue Jean d'Ardenne 50 (formerly rue d'Orléans 42), Ixelles
sources: persee.fr, 'Ixelles dans la vie et l'œuvre de Karl Marx'
histoiresdixelles.wordpress.com, '1846-48: Karl Marx habite rue Jean d'Ardenne'

stops.name: Grand-Place, the Swan: the speech on free trade
stops.campa: In the gilded guildhall of the butchers called the Maison du Cygne on the Grand-Place, the Swan, where the Democratic Association of Brussels meets and has elected Marx its vice-president, he delivers, on the ninth of January, his address on free trade. The doctors of protection and the doctors of the market both promise the workman bread; Marx accepts free trade with a terrible courtesy, because it widens the world market, sharpens every contradiction, and hurries the deluge. The German Workers' Society sings and lectures in these same rooms. Under the gilding, the spectre is drafting itself.
stops.quote: It is in this revolutionary sense alone, gentlemen, that I vote in favour of free trade.
stops.quote_source: Speech on the Question of Free Trade, Democratic Association of Brussels, 9 January 1848
suggested_refs: La Maison du Cygne on the Grand-Place, meeting hall of the Democratic Association
sources: Discours sur la question du libre-échange (MECW vol. 6)

stops.name: Ixelles, writing the Manifesto
stops.campa: The Communist League, at its London congress in the winter, has commissioned from Marx and Engels a profession of faith; Engels has already scrapped the catechism form for a manifesto. Now, in the Ixelles house, against a deadline from London threatening further measures if the manuscript fails to arrive by the first of February, Marx writes through the January nights, condensing a decade of theory into forty pages of black lightning. The manuscript goes to the printer in Liverpool Street days before Paris rises. History, for once, keeps the appointment: the book and the revolution appear in the same week.
stops.quote: A spectre is haunting Europe — the spectre of communism.
stops.quote_source: Manifesto of the Communist Party, February 1848
suggested_refs: The green-wrappered first edition of the Manifest der Kommunistischen Partei, London, February 1848
sources: Manifesto of the Communist Party (MECW vol. 6)
Central Authority of the Communist League to the Brussels circle, 24 January 1848
avanti4.be, 'Quand Marx rédigeait le Manifeste à Bruxelles'

stops.name: Brussels, the arrest at the Bois Sauvage and the expulsion
stops.campa: Paris has overthrown its king, and Brussels panics. On the third of March King Leopold signs the expulsion of Karl Marx within twenty-four hours; that same midnight police break into the family's rooms at the Bois Sauvage, where the trunks already stand packed, and take him to the Amigo prison beside the town hall. Jenny, seeking him, is seized in the street and locked among prostitutes till morning. Marched to the frontier, the family carries in its luggage the invitation of Flocon of the Provisional Government: tyranny has banished him, free France opens her doors. They take the Paris train.
suggested_refs: The Amigo lock-up beside the Hôtel de Ville of Brussels, where Marx and Jenny spent the night of expulsion
sources: Marx's account in La Réforme, 12 March 1848 (MECW vol. 6)
Jenny Marx, 'Short Sketch of an Eventful Life'

stops.name: Cologne, the Neue Rheinische Zeitung, organ of democracy
stops.campa: From revolutionary Paris, where he drafted the Demands of the Communist Party in Germany, Marx re-enters Prussia in April and raises in Cologne the Neue Rheinische Zeitung, Organ der Demokratie, himself editor-in-chief and dictator of the editorial room by cheerful confession of all hands. The first number appears the first of June. When Paris drowns the June insurgents in blood and the respectable shareholders flee, the paper alone raises the red flag of the defeated, and its greatest leader is written for the fallen of the barricades. Circulation climbs; prosecutors begin collecting the issues.
stops.quote: The workers of Paris were overwhelmed by superior strength, but they were not subdued. They have been defeated, but their enemies are vanquished.
stops.quote_source: Neue Rheinische Zeitung, 'The June Revolution', 29 June 1848
suggested_refs: The masthead of the Neue Rheinische Zeitung, Organ der Demokratie, Cologne 1848
sources: Engels, 'Marx and the Neue Rheinische Zeitung' (1884)

stops.name: Cologne, before the jury: the trial of the press
stops.campa: Twice in two days of February Marx stands before Rhenish juries: for insulting the public prosecutor in print, and for incitement to armed resistance during the tax-refusal campaign of November. He turns the dock into a lectern: the law they invoke is the corpse of a constitution the Crown itself has torn up, and when crown and assembly both appeal to the sword, it is the sword that decides. The jurors acquit him on every count, and their foreman thanks the accused for his instructive lecture. The government, beaten at law, reaches for the passport office.
stops.quote: The first duty of the press now is to undermine all the foundations of the existing political state of affairs.
stops.quote_source: Speech in his defence before the Cologne jury, February 1849
suggested_refs: The published record of the two Cologne press trials of February 1849
sources: The First Trial of the Neue Rheinische Zeitung (MECW vol. 8)

stops.name: Cologne, the red number
stops.campa: The counter-revolution has won everywhere, and on the sixteenth of May the government expels the stateless editor from Prussia. The Neue Rheinische Zeitung dies as no newspaper ever died: its final number of the nineteenth of May is printed entirely in red ink, carrying Freiligrath's farewell poem and the editors' warning to the workers of Cologne against any hopeless rising. Twenty thousand copies sell; collectors fight for the sheets while the presses are still warm. The editors scatter, Engels to the Baden rising, Marx toward Paris, the red flag folded into a page of newsprint.
stops.quote: Their last word everywhere and always will be: emancipation of the working class!
stops.quote_source: Neue Rheinische Zeitung, final (red) issue, 19 May 1849
suggested_refs: The red-printed final issue of the Neue Rheinische Zeitung, 19 May 1849
sources: Neue Rheinische Zeitung No. 301, 19 May 1849 (MECW vol. 9)
Engels, 'Marx and the Neue Rheinische Zeitung' (1884)

stops.name: Paris, Monsieur Ramboz and the marshes of Morbihan
stops.campa: He slips into a Paris under the reaction, cholera in the streets, lodging in the rue de Lille under the name Monsieur Ramboz, waiting for the next wave of the revolution that does not come. In July the police unmask him; the ministry offers him residence: in the Morbihan, the malarial flats of Brittany. Marx recognizes the geography of the offer and declines to die of it. On the twenty-fourth of August he sails for England, where Jenny, pregnant and penniless, follows with the three children in September. He believes the exile will last months. It lasts the rest of his life.
stops.quote: I am expelled to the Département du Morbihan, the Pontine marshes of France... So I am leaving France. In London I have the positive prospect of founding a German journal.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Engels, Paris, 23 August 1849
suggested_refs: The rue de Lille lodging of 'Monsieur Ramboz', summer 1849
sources: Jenny Marx, 'Short Sketch of an Eventful Life'

stops.name: London, landfall in the city of fog
stops.campa: The Boulogne steamer lands the thirty-one-year-old exile in the one city of Europe that asks no papers of its refugees. London swallows him among the wreckage of every defeated revolution, Germans, French, Hungarians, Poles, quarrelling in the smoke of Soho. The family takes rooms in Chelsea in Anderson Street; Guido, the fourth child, is born in November, a sickly babe of the crisis year. Within months the landlady's bailiffs will seize the beds while Jenny stands in the street with the children. Marx still expects the revolution by spring, and drills the League for its return.
suggested_refs: Anderson Street, Chelsea, first London address and first London eviction
sources: Jenny Marx, 'Short Sketch of an Eventful Life'

stops.name: Bloomsbury, the ticket to the British Museum
stops.campa: In June 1850 the reader's ticket is issued, and the great dome of the Museum's reading room becomes his true address for thirty years. Seat by seat with clergymen, cranks and lexicographers, the exile reads the Economist back through its files, the blue books of factory inspectors, currency, chemistry, rent: the whole confession that England writes about itself and never reads. Here the revolutionist of 1848 turns himself, deliberately, into the anatomist of capital: since the torrent has ebbed, he will map the sea-bed. The waiters of history are told they must wait for the science.
stops.quote: The enormous amount of material relating to the history of political economy assembled in the British Museum, the fact that London is a convenient vantage point for the observation of bourgeois society... induced me to start again from the very beginning.
stops.quote_source: Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, 1859
suggested_refs: The round Reading Room of the British Museum, his working seat for three decades
sources: British Museum reader's ticket records, June 1850

stops.name: Soho, Great Windmill Street: the split in the League
stops.campa: Above the Red Lion in Great Windmill Street, where the Manifesto had been commissioned three winters before, the Communist League tears itself in two on the fifteenth of September. Willich and Schapper want the revolution now, by will and gunpowder; Marx tells the workmen the terrible arithmetic of patience: that they may have decades of struggle to pass through, not merely to change the world but to make themselves fit to rule it. The majority follows him into the long view; the minority into conspiracies and duels. He withdraws to the Museum and the desert years.
stops.quote: You will have to go through 15, 20, 50 years of civil wars and national struggles not only to bring about a change in society but also to change yourselves, and prepare yourselves for the exercise of political power.
stops.quote_source: To the Communist League Central Authority, 15 September 1850, as recorded in Revelations Concerning the Communist Trial in Cologne
suggested_refs: The meeting room over the Red Lion, Great Windmill Street, Soho
sources: Minutes of the London Central Authority, 15 September 1850 (MECW vol. 10)
David McLellan, Karl Marx: His Life and Thought

stops.name: Soho, 28 Dean Street: the two rooms of poverty
stops.campa: In December 1850 the family crowds into two rooms above the Italian cook's at 28 Dean Street, Soho, and stays six years. A Prussian spy climbs the stairs and files his inventory: broken furniture, an inch of dust, manuscripts and children's toys on one table, and in the middle of it the most dangerous mind in Europe, cordial, hospitable, master of the conversation. Here Guido dies, and Franziska, and in 1855 the beloved boy Edgar in his father's arms; here Lenchen Demuth's son Freddy is born and carried away; here the Eighteenth Brumaire is written: tragedy, then farce.
stops.quote: I have already had my share of bad luck, but only now do I know what real unhappiness is... Amid all the fearful torments I have recently had to endure, the thought of you and your friendship has always sustained me.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Engels after Edgar's death, April 1855
suggested_refs: The house at 28 Dean Street, Soho, marked with its plaque above the restaurant
sources: Prussian agent's report on the Dean Street household, 1852
The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte (MECW vol. 11)

stops.name: Kentish Town, 9 Grafton Terrace: writing about money without any
stops.campa: A small inheritance of Jenny's lifts the family out of Soho in October 1856 to a new-built terrace house below Hampstead Heath, with real furniture and a doorbell: respectability maintained on Engels's postal orders and the pawnshop's calendar. Through nights of toothache and creditors Marx compresses fifteen years of Museum notebooks into the Grundrisse and then the Critique of Political Economy, whose manuscript is finished before he can afford the stamps to post it to Berlin. The Sunday walks on the Heath, with songs and Shakespeare recited to the daughters, are the family's one unbroken feast.
stops.quote: The unfortunate manuscript is finished, but cannot be sent off as I don't have a farthing for postage and insurance... I don't suppose anyone has ever written about 'money' when so short of the stuff.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Engels, 21 January 1859
suggested_refs: 9 (now 46) Grafton Terrace, Kentish Town, house of the Grundrisse

stops.name: Covent Garden, St Martin's Hall: the International is founded
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of September a crowded meeting of English trade unionists, French mutualists, and exiles of all nations in St Martin's Hall, Long Acre, founds the International Working Men's Association. Marx, invited almost as an afterthought, sits silent on the platform, a mute figure, he reports to Engels, and is elected to the committee, where within weeks he quietly writes the Inaugural Address and the Rules, threading revolution through resolutions that a London carpenter and a Paris bronze-worker can both sign. This time, he knows, real forces are in the room. The dead season is over.
stops.quote: The emancipation of the working classes must be conquered by the working classes themselves.
stops.quote_source: General Rules of the International Working Men's Association, October 1864
suggested_refs: St Martin's Hall, Long Acre, birthplace of the First International
sources: Inaugural Address and General Rules of the IWMA (MECW vol. 20)

stops.name: Hamburg, the manuscript delivered to Otto Meissner
stops.campa: Carrying the manuscript of the first volume of Capital in his own hands, Marx crosses a storm-whipped North Sea, standing on deck through the worst of it, exultant, and lands in Hamburg on the twelfth of April. In the Bergstraße he delivers to the publisher Otto Meissner the fruit of twenty years of the Museum, of carbuncles, pawnshops and dead children. While the type is set he stays at Kugelmann's in Hanover, reading proofs; on the second of September the book is out. He has, he says, sacrificed health, happiness and family to complete it; he does not repent.
stops.quote: It is without question the most terrible missile that has yet been hurled at the heads of the bourgeoisie (landowners included).
stops.quote_source: Letter to Johann Philipp Becker, April 1867
suggested_refs: The first edition of Das Kapital, Verlag von Otto Meissner, Hamburg 1867
sources: marx200.org, 'Karl Marx und die Drucklegung des Kapital 1867 in Hamburg'

stops.name: Maitland Park, 1 Modena Villas: the Commune and the red terror doctor
stops.campa: From the comfortable study at Modena Villas, Maitland Park, where Engels's generosity has made houses now, Marx watches Paris raise the Commune, and two days after its last barricade falls he reads to the General Council The Civil War in France, his funeral oration and battle-standard in one. The pamphlet runs through three editions in weeks, and the recluse of the Reading Room wakes to find himself the most calumniated man in London, the Red Terror Doctor, chief of the International in every ministry's imagination. He answers the notoriety with interviews, cigars, and the second volume, never finished.
stops.quote: Working men's Paris, with its Commune, will be forever celebrated as the glorious harbinger of a new society.
stops.quote_source: The Civil War in France, read to the General Council, 30 May 1871
suggested_refs: The Civil War in France, third edition, London 1871
sources: The Civil War in France (MECW vol. 22)
Minutes of the IWMA General Council, 30 May 1871

stops.name: The Hague, the Concordia hall: the only congress
stops.campa: For the only time in the International's life, Marx himself attends its congress, in the Concordia dance-hall in the Lombardstraat of The Hague, the first week of September. Crowds gather outside to see the monster of the newspapers pass: a grey-maned lion with a monocle, arm in arm with Jenny. Inside, five days of siege warfare against Bakunin's invisible empire end with the anarchist expelled and, by Marx's own motion, the General Council removed beyond reach to New York. He has won the battle and, knowing it, buried the Association with full honours in open sea.
suggested_refs: The Concordia hall in the Lombardstraat, The Hague, floor of the 1872 congress
sources: nl.wikipedia.org, 'Haags congres van de Eerste Internationale'

stops.name: Amsterdam, the speech on the peaceful road
stops.campa: The Sunday after the congress, Marx speaks to some hundred and fifty members of the Amsterdam section in a dance-hall off the Sarphatistraat: his last speech to a workers' assembly on the Continent. He defends the New York decision, salutes the Commune's dead, and lays down the distinction that a century will quarrel over: the goal is one, but the roads differ by country, where institutions allow it, in America, in England, perhaps in Holland, the workers may attain their end by peaceful means; elsewhere the lever must be force. Then the old lion goes home to his books.
stops.quote: We do not deny that there are countries — such as America, England, and if I were more familiar with your institutions, I would perhaps also add Holland — where the workers can attain their goal by peaceful means.
stops.quote_source: Speech on the Hague Congress, Amsterdam, 8 September 1872
suggested_refs: The report of the Amsterdam speech of 8 September 1872 in La Liberté

stops.name: Karlsbad: Herr Charles Marx, Privatier, at the Germania
stops.campa: Liver ailing, nerves worn, the author of Capital arrives on the twenty-second of August at the little Hotel Germania on the Schlossberg of Karlsbad, registered as Charles Marx, private gentleman, of London, with his youngest daughter Eleanor. The Austrian police shadow the private gentleman politely through three successive summers and report, with disappointment, that he rises at six, drinks his seven prescribed glasses at the Sprudel, walks the wooded terraces, and conspires with no one. The cure works; the carbuncles retreat. Among the archdukes and bankers taking the waters walks, unrecognized, their appointed end.
suggested_refs: The Karl Marx monument on the Schlossberg at Karlovy Vary, facing the site of the Germania
sources: Egon Erwin Kisch, 'Karl Marx in Karlsbad'
Austrian police reports on the spa guest Marx, 1874-1876

stops.name: Maitland Park Road, the death of Jenny
stops.campa: In the house at 41 Maitland Park Road, on the second of December, Jenny Marx dies of cancer of the liver, sixty-seven years old, the baron's daughter who chose the Moor and the pawnshops and never repented her wager. Marx, himself prostrate with pleurisy in the next room, is forbidden by the doctor to rise; their last words to each other are gay. On the day she dies Engels says the thing everyone remembers: the Moor has died as well. He is not permitted to follow her coffin to Highgate. The lamp of the household is out.
suggested_refs: Jenny von Westphalen's grave at Highgate, which her husband was too ill to attend

stops.name: Algiers, the Pension Victoria and the sacrificed beard
stops.campa: Chasing sunlight for his ravaged lungs, the widower sails to Africa, the only time in his life he leaves Europe, and from the twentieth of February to the second of May lodges at the Pension Victoria on the heights of Mustapha Supérieur, above the bay of Algiers. It rains as it has not rained in years; he watches the Arabs in the courts and cafés and writes to Engels of their democracy of bearing, nobler in rags than any European. On the twenty-seventh of April he sits for his last photograph, and next day gives beard and mane to an Algerian barber.
stops.quote: Because of the sun I have done away with my prophet's beard and my crowning glory, but in deference to my daughters I had myself photographed before offering up my hair on the altar of an Algerian barber.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Engels, Algiers, 28 April 1882
suggested_refs: The last photograph of Marx, taken by E. Dutertre at Algiers, 27 April 1882
sources: marcellomusto.org, 'Algiers 1882: The Last Journey of Marx'

stops.name: Ventnor, 1 St Boniface Gardens, the little paradise
stops.campa: By way of Monte Carlo, his daughter Jenny's house at Argenteuil, the sulphur baths of Enghien and the Lake of Geneva at Vevey, the sick man comes at the end of October to winter under the chalk downs of the Isle of Wight, at 1 St Boniface Gardens above Ventnor, where he had once called the island a little paradise. Fog and bronchitis besiege him instead. Here, on the eleventh of January, the telegram comes that Jennychen, his firstborn, is dead at thirty-eight. He leaves for London the same day, carrying, he says, his sentence with him.
stops.quote: The island is a little paradise.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Engels from the Isle of Wight, 1874
suggested_refs: The blue plaque at 1 St Boniface Gardens, Ventnor, marking his last two winters
sources: Marx to Engels, Isle of Wight letters (MECW)
Marcello Musto, The Last Years of Karl Marx

stops.name: Maitland Park Road, the armchair by the fire
stops.campa: On the fourteenth of March, at a quarter to three in the afternoon, Engels arrives at 41 Maitland Park Road for his daily visit and finds the house in tears. Lenchen had gone up minutes before: the Moor, left alone for two minutes, sits in his armchair by the study fire, gone quietly in his sleep, the unfinished manuscripts of the second and third volumes stacked around him like unfired ammunition. Mankind, Engels writes that night, is shorter by a head, and by the greatest head of its time. The greatest living thinker has ceased to think.
stops.quote: Go on, get out! Last words are for fools who haven't said enough.
stops.quote_source: His last recorded words, to his housekeeper Helene Demuth, as the tradition tells it
suggested_refs: The study armchair at 41 Maitland Park Road, in which the Moor was found

stops.name: Highgate, the grave and the graveside prophecy
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of March eleven mourners stand in the rain at Highgate as Karl Marx is laid in Jenny's grave. Engels speaks over the earth: as Darwin discovered the law of development of organic nature, so Marx discovered the law of development of human history; his name will endure through the ages, and so also will his work. The prophecy of the smallest funeral in London comes true beyond measure: seventy-one years later the grave is moved up the path and crowned with the bronze head, and the stone takes the eleventh thesis and the Manifesto's last cry for epitaph.
suggested_refs: The Marx tomb at Highgate Cemetery, inscribed WORKERS OF ALL LANDS UNITE
sources: Engels, 'Speech at the Grave of Karl Marx', 17 March 1883 (MECW vol. 24)
